title: ASML’s Strong Orders Signal Staying Power for the AI Boom
gist: ASML reported Q3 sales of EUR 11.7B and net profit of EUR 4.96B, raised its 2026 sales outlook to EUR 44-45B, and says customers are asking about 2029-2030 machine slots while demand for advanced tools may exceed supply through 2028. The piece argues this supports the construction phase of the AI boom but not the returns on it.

insights.claim: ASML reported third-quarter sales of EUR 11.7 billion and net profit of EUR 4.96 billion, and raised its annual sales outlook to EUR 44-45 billion.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Hard print confirming litho demand strength; a baseline for judging later guidance revisions.
insights.locator: ASML's latest results offer fresh evidence

insights.claim: Customers are expressing interest in ordering ASML machines for 2029 and even 2030, implying semiconductor expansion plans extend well beyond the current spending cycle.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Multi-year forward interest extends visibility for equipment suppliers far past current-cycle capex.
insights.quote: Customers are expressing interest in ordering machines for 2029 and even 2030

insights.claim: ASML says demand for its advanced equipment could exceed available production through 2028, and it is examining capacity expansion beyond previously announced increases plus upgrades that let existing machines produce more chips.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Supply, not demand, is the binding constraint on advanced equipment; watch capacity-expansion announcements and tool-upgrade revenue.

themes.theme: Read-through to the AI infrastructure chain

insights.claim: ASML is an early window into AI's physical build-out because chipmakers must secure equipment, build fabs and raise output before additional computing capacity can be deployed; orders years ahead therefore signal confidence in sustained advanced-chip demand.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Equipment orders lead chip output, which leads compute deployment; use ASML as a leading indicator of the AI cycle.

insights.claim: Continued factory expansion could sustain demand across chip manufacturers, equipment suppliers and data-centre builders, even if individual companies see uneven results.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Supports a picks-and-shovels view of the network over single-name bets.
insights.locator: For investors, that supports the argument

insights.claim: Strong equipment demand does not establish that every AI investment will earn attractive returns; buying machines reflects expectations about future business and cannot guarantee they prove correct.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Capex strength is not evidence of return on capital; separate construction-phase signals from monetisation signals.
insights.quote: Purchasing machines reflects expectations about future business

insights.claim: Long delivery times may push customers to reserve capacity early, making distant order interest harder to interpret as true end demand.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Discount far-dated order interest for placeholder reservations when sizing demand.

insights.claim: The debate may shift from whether AI spending continues to whether the resulting capacity earns enough; the next test is whether businesses and consumers generate sufficient demand for AI services to justify the infrastructure being built over the coming years.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Monitor AI service revenue and utilisation as the next phase of the thesis, rather than more capex headlines.
